title: Technical deep dive: Llama/Mistral/Qwen tuning (HelixAI)
summary: Redwood SE walked HelixAI through model-specific runtime knobs for Llama, Mistral, and Qwen families. Focus on KV cache sizing, batching policies, quantization trade-offs, MoE routing overhead, and RoPE scaling for long context. Agreed next steps: share quantization benchmarks, run kernel profiling, and provision a small dedicated trial for end-to-end latency tests.
next_steps: Redwood to send quantization benchmarking spreadsheet and prior evals (Alex)
Schedule kernel-level profiling session with HelixAI SREs (Priya)
Share SOC 2 + network diagram and VPC deployment checklist (Alex)
Provision 1-week Dedicated trial (3 GPUs) for HelixAI to run throughput/latency tests (Ops)
Follow-up call to review profiling results and decide on MoE routing thresholds (week of 2026-04-06)
action_items: Alex Kim: Send quantization benchmark sheet and model-run examples - due 2026-03-28
Priya Shah: Setup kernel profiling session and share profiler instructions - due 2026-04-01

transcript: Meeting header: 2026-03-25 15:00 UTC | Duration: ~62 minutes | Attendees: Alex Kim, Priya Shah (Redwood) — Daniel Park, Sara Nguyen, Liam O'Connor (HelixAI)

[00:00] Alex Kim: Hey everyone, thanks for joining. quick agenda — Priya will do a deep technical walkthrough on runtime knobs for Llama, Mistral, Qwen, then we'll talk MoE routing and RoPE scaling, and end with next steps.
[00:12] Liam O'Connor: Thanks Alex. we're most worried about tail latency on customer-facing chat and the cost per 1000 requests.
[00:20] Daniel Park: our stack is k8s on GCP, VPC peering to a private subnet. we might go on prem for some customers later.

[00:28] Priya Shah: OK — good context. want to start with the KV cache and batching because those are the highest ROI for you. quick note — some names might be off in the transcript e.g., our internal product called Redwood Dedicated sometimes shows up as Red wood Dedicated in the notes.

[00:45] Priya Shah: For Llama-family models the KV cache growth is linear with sequence length — so for long context you either increase GPU memory or aggressively evict prefix keys. We usually recommend prefix caching for high-repeat prompts, full KV for chat sessions where you need continuity.
[01:10] Daniel Park: can you quantify memory per token? like for a 13B Llama with 2048 context, how much RAM does the KV cache take on A100?

[01:18] Priya Shah: ballpark: ~1.5-2 bytes per key entry per head per token after quantized kernels, but that varies. for a 13B model it's roughly 1.2-1.6GB for 2k context depending on kv format and whether we store in fp16 or q4. the profiling sheet I'll send has exact numbers — but expect that to scale linearly with sequence.
[01:45] Sara Nguyen: we saw some weird spikes where tail latency increased after ~1k tokens, was that likely kv thrashing?

[01:52] Priya Shah: yes, typically that's either cache eviction pressure or kernel selection shifting to slower paths when seq length crosses a threshold. we tune a breakpoint for kernel selection — e.g., <=512 use optimized fused kernels, >512 switch to a different path which costs more per token. you can also set a hard max context we accept at the API layer to avoid that.
[02:15] Alex Kim: (interruption) also batching policies matter — small batches keep latency low but raise cost per token. will dig into that next.

[02:22] [02:22] Priya Shah: For throughput you want continuous batching with dynamic floor — we recommend adaptive batching that grows up to 128 tokens or N requests based on latency SLO. for HelixAI with 99th percentile <250ms target, we saw the sweet spot at batch sizes ~8-16 on GA100 equivalents. note this depends heavily on prompt length distribution.
[02:52] Daniel Park: what's the impact of quantization on throughput vs quality for these families?

[02:59] Priya Shah: Mistral reacts better to aggressive quantization (q4/q5) than some Llama variants; Qwen holds up well too. but MoE and some custom layers are sensitive. our quantization bench will show perplexity/delta BLEU for your eval prompts. expect 10-20% throughput gain from int8-like quant paths with small quality tradeoffs for many tasks.
[03:30] Liam O'Connor: you mentioned MoE — we have a prototype MoE model with gating but cost spikes when the router routes to many experts. how do you recommend controlling that?

[03:38] Priya Shah: MoE routing costs are real — the router overhead and cross-expert communication can blow up latency even if FLOPs are lower. options: cap the number of active experts per token (top-k gating), use routing thresholds, or hybrid: fallback to dense model for short contexts. also batching MoE is trickier because tokens route differently; we have a routing-aware batcher in Redwood that groups tokens by expert to reduce cross-comm. but that increases scheduling complexity.
[04:05] Daniel Park: is there a simple heuristic for when MoE is worthwhile?

[04:10] Priya Shah: yes — MoE helps when you need high capacity for diverse outputs but can tolerate some variance in latency. set a cost budget: if effective throughput cost per token (including router overhead) < equivalent dense model cost, it's beneficial. in practice you should simulate with your prompt distribution. we'll help run a small benchmark on Dedicated to compare.
[04:35] Sara Nguyen: about RoPE scaling — our use case includes long-context documents up to 8k tokens. we saw generation quality degrade when we scaled RoPE. any tips?

[04:45] Priya Shah: RoPE scaling is subtle; for models like Qwen and some Llama forks, you want to use scaled RoPE or ALiBi-like adjustments depending on training. simple rule: if your model was trained with RoPE at 2k, scaling to 8k without fine-tuning can cause drift. you can mitigate with positional interpolation (interpolate rotary frequencies) or rebase embeddings. we recently did a test where interpolating rotary frequencies recovered ~90% of long-context quality without full fine-tune. we'll share the experiment notes.
[05:12] Alex Kim: (to Daniel) Does HelixAI plan to extend contexts to 8k in prod, or is that exploratory?
[05:18] Daniel Park: planning for some customers, but it's not universal. primary target is 1k-2k, with a few pilots at 8k.
[05:25] Priya Shah: then recommend hybrid approach — serve 2k as default and enable 8k on canary for users who need it; set separate SLOs. that avoids paying for high memory usage across the board.
[05:40] Liam O'Connor: curious on VPC/on-prem constraints — if we go private, how much extra latency do you see for KMS calls and network egress?

[05:48] Priya Shah: KMS calls for encryption and signing are usually async and cached; overhead is small if you use local HSM or regional KMS. network egress depends on topology — a VPC with peered subnet in same zone adds ~1-3ms; cross-region is heavier. Redwood Private offers an option to deploy inference nodes in your VPC to remove public egress. we'll provide the checklist.
[06:10] Sara Nguyen: any gotchas for on-prem GPU drivers? we've seen issues with cuDNN mismatches causing fallback to slower kernels.

[06:16] Priya Shah: absolutely — driver/kernel mismatch is one of the top causes of degraded performance. we maintain a validated stack (CUDA, cuDNN, NCCL) and will share the exact versions. during profiling we often find a single node with a different driver causing noise — our Ops template includes driver checks.
[06:32] Alex Kim: (notes) we'll share validated stack and profiler script. next, microbenchmarks — Priya run through a sample profiling trace?

[06:40] Priya Shah: sure — here's an excerpt from a 13B Qwen run we did: baseline dense single-token latency 12ms (512 context), with batching to 8, amortized per-token 3.5ms. after q4 quantization on weights, single-token latency dropped to ~9ms and amortized to 2.6ms. notable: at 1024 tokens we hit a kernel crossover and latency jumped ~30%. that crossover point differs per model and hardware.
[07:10] Daniel Park: any automation in Redwood for detecting crossover and switching kernels?

[07:14] Priya Shah: yes — runtime selects kernels based on heuristics and recent request sequence-length distribution. we also support a manual override per route if you want to force a particular kernel profile.
[07:28] Sara Nguyen: we have regulatory customers asking for audit logs and key rotation — how do you handle that in Private?

[07:34] Alex Kim: Redwood Private supports KMS integrations, audit logs, and can be configured to push logs to your SIEM. we also support role-based access and SSO (SAML). I'll attach our SOC 2 and architecture diagram.
[07:50] Liam O'Connor: For MoE routing — is it possible to cap routing latency per request? i.e. if router exceeds X ms, fall back to dense variant?

[07:58] Priya Shah: yes — you can set a per-request cost budget and fallback policy. we often set a hard router timeout and fallback to a dense model or smaller expert set. it's part of the smart routing features.
[08:10] Daniel Park: performance tuning aside, how do we measure quality regressions after quantization? we can't afford hallucination increases for answers to payments questions.

[08:17] Priya Shah: baseline is to run your evaluation suite — your canonical prompts — through both quant and baseline models and measure task-level metrics and safety checks. Redwood Optimize can run continuous evals and alert on regressions against preset thresholds. we'll include that in the trial.
[08:35] Alex Kim: (recap) agreed actions — send quant bench, schedule kernel profiling, spin up a small Dedicated trial. anything else?
[08:42] Daniel Park: can you also include guidance for batching configs in the docs — like sample configs for 99th p50 tradeoffs?
[08:49] Priya Shah: yes — I'll add sample configs for adaptive batching with recommended SLOs. also note we have a routing-aware batcher for MoE which requires slightly different configs.
[09:05] Sara Nguyen: quick question — for RoPE interpolation do you have a script or is it manual?
[09:11] Priya Shah: we have a reference script and a small adapter pipeline that does frequency interpolation; it's not magic but it helps. I'll attach it.
[09:20] Liam O'Connor: timeline — if we start the trial next week how quickly can we get meaningful numbers?

[09:25] Alex Kim: Ops can provision the Dedicated trial in 2-3 business days. with the profiling scripts and your prompt set, you can get initial throughput/latency numbers in a day or two. end-to-end benchmark in a week.

[09:38] Priya Shah: final technical note: for Qwen specifically watch out for tokenization differences — different tokenizers change effective prompt lengths which impacts KV size and batching behavior. always align tokenizers during eval.
[09:55] Daniel Park: noted. thanks Priya.
[10:00] Alex Kim: great — we'll follow up with the artifacts. thanks everyone. end of call.
(Artifacts referenced: quantization_bench_v2.xlsx (to be shared), kernel_profiling_instructions.md (to be shared), SOC2_and_arch_diagram.pdf (to be shared))
